lessons.title: Why and how we measure grain levels
lessons.html:
Why we measure grain levels

A silo must know how much grain is in each bin. The stock records say how much should be there (book stock). Measuring the level of grain in the bin shows how much is really there (physical stock). The two are compared to find mistakes, losses or theft. Levels are also needed to plan intake and dispatch: how much space is left, and how much can be loaded out.

What you measure

You measure the distance from a fixed point at the top of the bin, usually the roof hatch or a marked measuring point, down to the surface of the grain. This is called the ullage or empty space. The bin's height minus the empty space gives the height of the grain.

The silo has bin tables for each bin. They change a grain height into a volume or a mass. The grain's hectolitre mass (how heavy a set volume of that grain is) is used to change volume into tonnes.

Tools

  • Weighted measuring tape or sounding line.
  • Electronic level sensors or radar in some bins.
  • Torch.
  • Bin tables and recording sheet.
  • Radio or phone to stay in contact.

Grain surface shape

Grain does not lie flat. When filling, it makes a cone (heap) in the middle. When emptying from the bottom, it makes a funnel (dip) in the middle. You may have to measure at more than one point and use the average, or use the correction in the bin tables. Your supervisor will show you the method used at your site.

Example

Bin 7 is 30 m high. The tape shows 12 m of empty space from the measuring point. The grain height is 30 - 12 = 18 m. Pieter reads the bin table at 18 m for maize and records the tonnes.

lessons.title: Measuring safely and recording
lessons.html:
Measuring safely

Measuring grain levels means working on silo roofs and near open hatches. Falls and engulfment kill workers every year.

Safety rules

  • Get permission from your supervisor before going onto the roof. Follow the work-at-heights and permit rules.
  • Check the weather. Do not go on the roof in strong wind, rain or lightning.
  • Use the fixed ladders and walkways with rails. Wear a harness and clip on where required.
  • Never work alone. Your partner stays at the hatch and keeps radio contact with the control room.
  • Make sure no grain is being loaded or unloaded from that bin while you measure. Ask the control room to stop and lock out.
  • Never enter the bin or stand on the grain surface. Grain can collapse or flow and bury you.
  • Grain dust and fumigant gas can collect in bins. Do not lean into the hatch. Follow fumigation warning signs.
  • Close the hatch when you are finished.

Steps

  1. Note the bin number, date and time.
  2. Lower the weighted tape from the measuring point until the weight just touches the grain surface. The tape goes slack.
  3. Read the tape at the measuring point.
  4. Repeat at other points if your method needs it.
  5. Write down each reading straight away.
  6. Ask your partner to read it too and both sign.
  7. Use the bin table to find the tonnes, or hand the readings to the stock clerk.

Check your answer

Compare the tonnes with the book stock. A big difference may mean a reading error. Measure again before reporting. If it is still different, report it to your supervisor.

Key points

  • Measuring levels shows the physical stock in each bin.
  • Measure empty space from the fixed point and subtract from bin height.
  • Use bin tables to change height to tonnes.
  • Never enter a bin; work with a partner and stop grain movement first.
  • Record readings straight away and report big differences.
